case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Hawaii’s default rule criminalizing carrying firearms on another’s private property open to the public unless the carrier first obtains the owner’s affirmative consent violates the Second Amendment under Bruen’s text-and-history test (and related limits on a state’s ability to redefine property rights to burden a constitutional right).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. II (as incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment), and Hawaii’s statute imposing an affirmative-consent requirement for carrying firearms on private property (including property open to the public).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Second Amendment’s plain text covers public carry for self-defense, and Hawaii’s affirmative-consent default flips the presumption of lawful carry into presumptive criminality across large swaths of ordinary life (e.g., stores, gas stations, inns/taverns). Under Bruen, the State must justify that burden by pointing to a well-established historical tradition of analogous firearm regulation, which Petitioners say does not exist—founding-era rules for property open to the public and open fields generally presumed permission unless land was enclosed or notice was given. Petitioners also contend the State cannot evade the Second Amendment by ‘redefining’ property/trespass rules in a way that functionally suppresses arms-bearing, and that courts—not historians testifying as experts—must decide the legal meaning of historical statutes and whether Heller/McDonald/Bruen’s holdings control.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hawaii argues the law is a permissible accommodation between two fundamental rights: the right to bear arms and private owners’ right to exclude. On this view, the statute does not ban public carry generally; it allocates to property owners the choice whether firearms are allowed on their premises by requiring carriers to obtain express consent. Hawaii maintains that this is consistent with historical limitations on carrying on others’ property and with longstanding understandings of trespass and property law, and it emphasizes that its law is less restrictive than regimes that require written consent or irrebuttable presumptions because it allows on-the-spot oral consent (so, for example, a person can ask at a gas station). Hawaii also relies on historical sources it characterizes as close analogues (including Reconstruction-era enactments), contending that these demonstrate a tradition of restricting armed entry onto private premises absent permission.
key_precedents: District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008)
McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010)
New York State Rifle & Pistol Assn., Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022)
Herring v. United States, 955 F.2d 703 (11th Cir. 1992)
Commodores Entertainment Corp. v. McClary, 879 F.3d 1114 (11th Cir. 2018)

John Roberts.reasoning: The State’s best point remains the property-rights framing: legislatures may set trespass defaults that respect an owner’s right to exclude. But as Justice Kavanaugh stresses, an affirmative-consent regime for property held open to the public is not a neutral default; in practice it creates a permission-by-permission system that functions like a broad carry restriction across the modern public square, which Bruen requires the State to justify with a representative historical analogue it has not supplied. Justice Gorsuch’s invocation of Tyler v. Hennepin County usefully reinforces an anti-evasion principle—States cannot manipulate baseline entitlements to accomplish indirectly what they cannot do directly—though my conclusion does not depend on Tyler so long as we keep the holding narrow. I would therefore adhere to a limited ruling: invalidate Hawaii’s default ban as applied to premises open to the public while preserving proprietors’ ability to exclude by notice and leaving truly sensitive-place restrictions for separate analysis.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument would be that States may set default trespass rules reflecting owners’ right to exclude, so a no-carry default simply respects private property. But Bruen makes clear that once the Second Amendment’s text covers the conduct—bearing arms in ordinary public-facing places—the State must justify a broad criminal prohibition with a well-established historical analogue, and Hawaii’s opt-in regime functions as a de facto carry ban over the modern public square without a Founding-era tradition to match. Chief Justice Roberts’ narrower framing is sound: invalidating the affirmative-consent default as applied to property held open to the public preserves owners’ ability to forbid carry by notice while preventing the State from converting an enumerated right into presumptive criminality through baseline manipulation. The Tyler v. Hennepin County anti-evasion principle, invoked by Justice Gorsuch, reinforces that we should not allow a State to redefine property/trespass baselines to do indirectly what it cannot do directly under the Second and Fourteenth Amendments.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The State’s strongest counter is the property-rights framing—that owners have a right to exclude and the State may set a default rule requiring affirmative consent. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Hawaii is not merely vindicating private choice; it is converting a constitutional baseline into presumptive criminality across ordinary, publicly accessible commercial premises, which under Bruen demands a well-established historical analogue that Hawaii has not shown. Justice Thomas is right that the proffered history (anti-poaching trespass laws and scattered Reconstruction/Black Code measures) is not representative evidence of the Founding-era tradition needed to sustain a sweeping default carry ban in places the public is invited to enter. Tyler v. Hennepin County, invoked by several colleagues, reinforces the anti-evasion principle: a State cannot manipulate property-law baselines to sidestep constitutional scrutiny, and here the default rule functions as an end-run around Bruen’s rejection of broad “sensitive places” expansions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Respondent’s best point remains the property-rights baseline: the State says it is simply enforcing an owner’s right to exclude by presuming no consent to armed entry. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, when that presumption is imposed by the government across the ordinary places people must enter for daily life, it operates as a sweeping location-based carry restriction that Bruen requires the State to justify with a representative historical analogue—one Hawaii has not shown. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability concerns reinforce the real-world impact: a permission-by-permission regime predictably chills lawful self-defense and burdens those with the least capacity to navigate discretionary, piecemeal permissions. Tyler v. Hennepin County, invoked by Roberts and Thomas, strengthens my view that the State cannot evade constitutional limits by manipulating background property/trespass defaults to render an enumerated right presumptively criminal in the modern public square.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The State’s best point remains the property-rights framing: legislatures can define trespass defaults and thereby protect an owner’s right to exclude. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh stress, Bruen asks whether the State may make carry in the ordinary, public-facing commercial sphere presumptively criminal unless a citizen secures affirmative consent—an opt-in regime that functions like the broad “most places” prohibition Bruen rejected when it warned against relabeling ordinary life as “sensitive.” The cited historical analogues (anti-poaching trespass laws and scattered Reconstruction/Black Code measures) are too episodic and nonrepresentative to establish the kind of enduring tradition Bruen demands for flipping the baseline across vast categories of premises held open to the public. Tyler v. Hennepin County, invoked by Justice Gorsuch and others, reinforces (even if it is not strictly necessary to my conclusion) that States cannot manipulate background property baselines to evade a constitutional constraint—here, by converting routine public carry into default criminality.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best case is the property-right-to-exclude framing: that Hawaii is simply setting a neutral trespass default of “no guns unless invited.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Bruen does not permit a State to flip the baseline for an enumerated right across the ordinary places citizens are invited to enter, then back it with criminal penalties, absent a representative historical analogue—and Hawaii’s proffer (anti-poaching measures and scattered Reconstruction/Black Code-era enactments) is not the kind of enduring tradition Bruen demands. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability point reinforces the constitutional defect: a permission-by-permission regime for routine commerce operates as a functional carry ban, not ordinary enforcement of private choice. Tyler v. Hennepin County, invoked by Roberts and Thomas, supports the anti-evasion principle that the State cannot manipulate background property/trespass rules to accomplish indirectly what it cannot do directly under the Second and Fourteenth Amendments.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the property-rights framing—that Hawaii is simply enforcing an owner’s traditional right to exclude by making “no guns without consent” the default—but under Bruen the State still must identify a well-established historical analogue for imposing a criminal-law presumption against carry on property held open to the public. As Chief Justice Roberts persuasively emphasizes, flipping the baseline to an affirmative-consent regime across ordinary public-facing premises functions in practice like the kind of broad location-based carry restriction Bruen rejected when it warned against expanding “sensitive places” to cover most of public life. Justice Thomas’s critique of Hawaii’s historical analogues (anti-poaching laws and Reconstruction/Black Code outliers) reinforces that the State has not carried its burden to show a representative Founding/1868 tradition for this default rule. Tyler’s anti-evasion principle, noted by Roberts and Gorsuch, supports the institutionalist concern that States cannot repackage sweeping Second Amendment burdens as mere “trespass defaults” to achieve indirectly what they cannot do directly.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The State’s strongest argument remains the property-rights baseline—that owners may exclude and the legislature may set a default presumption of no consent—but under Bruen the question is whether the State may convert bearing arms in the ordinary, public-facing commercial sphere into presumptive criminality absent a representative historical analogue. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Hawaii’s opt-in regime for property held open to the public functions like an overbroad “sensitive places” expansion and cannot be justified by relabeling it as trespass; it is baseline manipulation aimed at suppressing an enumerated right rather than neutral enforcement of owners’ choices. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability concern reinforces the constitutional burden in practice: a permission-by-permission regime for routine errands is a functional carry ban inconsistent with the Second Amendment’s protection of “bearing” arms. Tyler v. Hennepin County, as Roberts and Justice Gorsuch note, supports the anti-evasion principle that States cannot redefine background entitlements to evade constitutional limits, and nothing in Hawaii’s historical citations (anti-poaching measures and Reconstruction outliers) supplies the well-established tradition Bruen requires.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The State’s best case remains the property-right-to-exclude framing, but as Chief Justice Roberts explains, Bruen places the historical-burden squarely on Hawaii to justify converting carry on premises held open to the public into presumptive criminality absent affirmative consent, and the cited analogues (anti-poaching/trespass measures and Reconstruction/Black Code outliers) are not representative of a sustained tradition. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability point reinforces the real-world consequence: a permission-by-permission regime for routine errands functions as a broad carry prohibition, not a neutral trespass baseline, and that practical sweep matters under a progressive pragmatist lens focused on how rules operate on the ground. Tyler v. Hennepin County, as several colleagues note (including Justice Gorsuch), supports the anti-evasion principle: the State cannot manipulate background property/trespass defaults to accomplish indirectly what it cannot do directly when an enumerated right is at stake. A narrow ruling limited to property open to the public—preserving owners’ ability to exclude through notice—best aligns doctrine with workable, fair procedure and avoids arbitrary or discriminatory enforcement dynamics.

John Roberts.reasoning: Bruen holds that once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers the conduct (bearing arms in ordinary public places), the State bears the burden to show a well-established historical tradition of analogous regulation, and it rejected efforts to expand “sensitive places” to broad categories of public congregation. Hawaii’s default rule makes armed entry onto most private property open to the public presumptively criminal absent affirmative consent, functionally resembling the overbreadth Bruen disapproved and lacking a clear founding-era analogue for open-to-the-public premises. While property owners retain a right to exclude, the State may not, by redefining background trespass/property defaults, impose a sweeping location-based carry restriction that burdens a constitutional right—an approach consistent with our refusal in other contexts to let government alter property baselines to evade constitutional limits (see Tyler v. Hennepin County). A narrow ruling invalidating this default-presumption as applied to property open to the public (while leaving intact the ability of owners to prohibit carry by notice and the State to regulate truly sensitive places) best respects precedent and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text protects the right to “bear” arms, which Bruen held includes a general right to carry handguns publicly for self-defense; Hawaii’s default rule makes that ordinary exercise presumptively criminal across vast swaths of daily life on property open to the public. Under Bruen’s text-and-history test, the State must identify a well-established founding-era tradition of analogous regulations, and the cited materials (e.g., an anti-poaching trespass measure and Reconstruction-era Black Code-type enactments) are outliers and not evidence of the Amendment’s original public meaning. Nor may a State evade an enumerated right by redefining background property/trespass defaults to impose a de facto carry ban, a principle consistent with our refusal to let States manipulate property concepts to sidestep constitutional constraints (see Tyler v. Hennepin County). Because Hawaii has not carried its burden to show a relevant historical analogue, the statute violates the Second Amendment as incorporated by the Fourteenth Amendment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text covers carrying firearms in public for self-defense, and Hawaii’s affirmative-consent default makes ordinary, ubiquitous destinations on private property held open to the public (stores, gas stations, inns) presumptively off-limits on pain of criminal punishment. Under Bruen, once the conduct is covered by the Amendment’s text, the State bears the burden to show a well-established historical analogue; Hawaii’s reliance on scattered Reconstruction-era enactments and outlier measures (including Black Codes) does not establish a representative tradition sufficient to justify turning most of public life into a de facto carry ban. Bruen also rejected broad location-based prohibitions untethered to a narrow, historically grounded ‘sensitive places’ category, and Hawaii’s rule is not limited to genuinely sensitive places. Nor may a State evade constitutional scrutiny by effectively redefining background property/trespass rules to burden a constitutional right, a principle consistent with the Court’s refusal to permit government manipulation of property concepts to defeat constitutional protections (see Tyler v. Hennepin County).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Hawaii’s affirmative-consent default makes ordinary public life on privately owned, publicly accessible property presumptively criminal for licensed carry, effectively converting broad swaths of the public sphere into off-limits zones—precisely the kind of end-run Bruen warned against when it rejected designating expansive areas as "sensitive places" without a sufficiently rooted historical tradition. Under Bruen’s text-and-history test, the State must show a well-established analogue for criminalizing carry on generally open commercial premises absent prior permission, and reliance on Reconstruction-era outliers such as Black Codes is not a “mainstream” tradition Bruen permits. Nor may a State “redefine” baseline property/trespass rules to impose a special, across-the-board disability on exercising a constitutional right, a point reinforced by Tyler v. Hennepin County’s insistence that States cannot manipulate property law definitions to evade constitutional constraints. Given the practical burdens on self-defense for ordinary people—especially those most vulnerable—and the absence of a persuasive historical analogue, the statute violates the Second Amendment as applied to private property open to the public.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s text covers the conduct—bearing arms in public for self-defense—the State bears the burden to "affirmatively prove" a representative historical tradition that justifies its restriction. Hawaii’s default rule effectively converts ordinary commercial premises open to the public into presumptively gun-free zones unless a citizen secures affirmative consent, a structure that functions like the “Manhattan-as-sensitive-place” regime Bruen rejected and threatens workability by making routine travel depend on ad hoc permissions. The analogues Hawaii emphasizes—especially isolated Reconstruction-era enactments such as an 1865 Louisiana Black Code and a distinct 1771 anti-poaching trespass law—look like outliers or mismatched regulations rather than the kind of mainstream tradition Bruen requires, and the State cannot evade the Second Amendment by recasting baseline property/trespass rules to burden an enumerated right (cf. Tyler v. Hennepin County’s refusal to let the government redefine property interests to avoid constitutional limits). Because Hawaii has not shown a sufficiently analogous, enduring tradition for this presumption-flipping regime on property open to the public, the statute violates the Second Amendment as incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text protects the right to “bear Arms,” which Heller and Bruen confirm includes ordinary public carry for self-defense, and Hawaii’s default rule converts that right into presumptive criminality across most places the public routinely must go (stores, restaurants, gas stations) absent affirmative consent. Under Bruen’s text-and-history test, the State must identify a well-established historical analogue at the Founding or in 1868 for a default no-carry rule on private property held open to the public, and the asserted materials (including Reconstruction-era outliers like Black Codes) do not supply the needed “mainstream” tradition. Nor may a State evade a constitutional right by “redefining” background property/trespass rules to impose a functional ban—an approach we have rejected in other constitutional settings, see Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023). Because Hawaii cannot carry its historical burden and the law effectively negates the public-carry right recognized in Bruen, it violates the Second Amendment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s text covers ordinary public carry for self-defense, Hawaii must justify its affirmative-consent default with a well-established historical analogue; the State’s cited sources (largely anti-poaching and Reconstruction/Black Code outliers) do not show a mainstream tradition of criminalizing carry on private property open to the public absent express permission. The law flips the background presumption for common venues (stores, gas stations, inns) from lawful carry to presumptive criminality, which is a substantial, practically unworkable burden on the right to “bear” arms recognized in Heller and incorporated in McDonald. Hawaii may protect owners’ right to exclude through ordinary trespass rules and posted-notice regimes, but it cannot redefine property/trespass defaults in a way that functionally suppresses a constitutional right, consistent with the Court’s general insistence that States cannot manipulate baseline property rules to evade constitutional constraints (see Tyler). Respect for precedent and administrability favor invalidating this sweeping default prohibition while leaving intact targeted, historically grounded restrictions (e.g., on truly sensitive places or on entry into private dwellings).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text protects bearing arms in public for self-defense, and Hawaii’s statute makes that conduct presumptively criminal across vast swaths of ordinary life by defaulting all private property open to the public to a no-carry rule absent affirmative consent. Under Bruen’s text-and-history framework, Hawaii must identify a well-established, representative historical tradition of analogous regulations; reliance on Reconstruction-era outliers such as Black Codes cannot supply the requisite tradition, and the State’s property-rights framing cannot evade a direct burden on the right to bear arms. Nor may the State effectively “redefine” background property/trespass rules to impose a categorical location-based prohibition that would otherwise fail Bruen, a principle consistent with our refusal to accept governmental recharacterizations of property interests to defeat constitutional constraints (see Tyler v. Hennepin County). Because Hawaii’s affirmative-consent default is not meaningfully limited to historically recognized “sensitive places” as discussed in Bruen and operates as a broad default ban, it violates the Second Amendment as incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers the conduct (carrying a handgun for self-defense in ordinary public-facing places), Hawaii bears the burden to show a well-established historical tradition supporting its affirmative-consent default as applied to private property open to the public; the record described here relies heavily on scattered, late-enacted laws and an 1865 Louisiana Black Code outlier, which Bruen instructs courts not to treat as establishing the relevant tradition. By criminalizing carry in the ubiquitous commercial venues where people ‘live and move’ unless a proprietor affirmatively opts in, the statute functionally converts a constitutional baseline into presumptive criminality and imposes practical obstacles inconsistent with Heller’s recognition of an operative right to armed self-defense and McDonald’s incorporation of that right against the States. The State’s “property-rights” framing cannot do the work because a State may not manipulate background property/trespass baselines to evade an enumerated right, a principle reflected in Tyler v. Hennepin County’s limits on government redefining property entitlements and echoed by the anti-evasion logic implicit in Bruen’s sensitive-places analysis. Procedural fairness and administrability concerns reinforce this conclusion: requiring citizens to seek individualized permission for routine errands invites arbitrary enforcement and predictable chilling of constitutionally protected conduct across large swaths of public life.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Hawaii’s default rule criminalizing the carrying of firearms on private property open to the public unless the owner gives affirmative consent violates the Second Amendment under Bruen’s text-and-history test and impermissibly redefines property rights to burden a constitutional right.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. II (as incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment), and Hawaii’s statute/regime establishing a presumption that carrying firearms on private property (including property open to the public) is unlawful absent affirmative owner consent (and related “sensitive place”/location-based restrictions as litigated).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Hawaii’s law directly regulates and effectively nullifies ordinary public carry by making it presumptively criminal to bear arms on vast swaths of privately owned but publicly accessible places (e.g., stores, gas stations, inns/taverns), unless individualized permission is obtained. Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers public carry for self-defense, the State must show a well-established historical analogue from the founding-era tradition; generalized public-safety or modern policy evidence cannot substitute for that historical showing (citing McDonald’s rejection of empirical balancing). Petitioners also contend Hawaii cannot avoid Second Amendment scrutiny by characterizing the law as merely ‘protecting property owners’ right to exclude,’ because the State is redefining baseline property/trespass rules in a way that burdens a constitutional right—analogous to the principle that government may not manipulate background property rules to evade other constitutional constraints (as discussed at argument with reference to Tyler v. Hennepin County). They further press that courts—not historians testifying as experts—must decide the legal meaning of historical statutes and traditions; expert testimony that amounts to legal conclusions about what Heller/McDonald/Bruen held or how to interpret founding-era laws should be excluded under Rule 702 principles.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hawaii argues the statute permissibly harmonizes two rights: the right to bear arms and private property owners’ right to exclude. In the State’s view, the law does not ban carry writ large; it sets a default rule that ensures owners have an on-the-spot opportunity to decide whether to allow firearms on their property, with oral consent available even absent posted signage. Hawaii seeks to defend the regime as consistent with historical practice and analogues concerning weapons restrictions on another’s property and regulations protecting possessory interests, and it resists the claim that the law functionally eliminates public carry because individuals can request permission. In historical argumentation, Hawaii appears to rely in part on post-Civil-War sources (including, as highlighted at argument, an 1865 Louisiana Black Code), contending those sources provide strong analogical support; petitioners and some Justices question whether such outlier or discriminatory laws can count as part of the ‘mainstream’ tradition Bruen requires.

McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010)
N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022)
Commodores Entertainment Corp. v. McClary, 879 F.3d 1114 (11th Cir. 2018)
United States v. Herring, 955 F.2d 703 (11th Cir. 1992)
Heller v. District of Columbia (Heller II), 670 F.3d 1244 (D.C. Cir. 2011) (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting) (as quoted)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Hawaii is simply setting a trespass-style default to vindicate owners’ common-law right to exclude, and that Tyler is inapposite because it concerned a taking rather than a Second Amendment burden. But under Bruen, once public carry is covered conduct, the State cannot avoid its historical-analogue burden by relabeling a statewide presumption of criminality as “property law,” especially when it applies to the ordinary commercial premises where people “lawfully go” and thus functions, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, like a broad place-based prohibition absent affirmative opt-in. Tyler’s relevance is modest but real in the anti-evasion sense emphasized by Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan: a State cannot manipulate baseline legal rules in a targeted way that uniquely burdens a constitutional right and thereby sidesteps the required constitutional justification. I therefore favor a narrow disposition (as Justice Gorsuch suggests) invalidating the affirmative-consent default as applied to private property held open to the public while preserving owners’ ability to exclude by notice and leaving sensitive-places questions for a later case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Hawaii is merely mediating the common-law right to exclude by setting a trespass-style default that preserves owner autonomy, rather than creating a “sensitive places” ban. But under Bruen the question is whether the State may, by statute, flip the baseline for premises held open to the public so that the ordinary act of bearing arms becomes presumptively criminal absent affirmative consent; that is a State-imposed burden on covered conduct, not simply private choice. As Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch note, Hawaii’s rule operates like a broad place-based prohibition across commonplace destinations, and the State has not identified a well-established founding-era tradition of a government-mandated consent-default for such public-facing commerce; postbellum outliers, including discriminatory Black Codes, cannot supply the requisite “mainstream” tradition. Tyler v. Hennepin County reinforces the anti-evasion principle: the State cannot manipulate background property/trespass rules to do indirectly what the Constitution forbids directly—here, functionally nullifying ordinary public carry by redefining the default.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that the statute merely implements private owners’ traditional right to exclude, but that characterization fails because Hawaii has not simply enforced ordinary trespass law—it has flipped the default and attached criminal liability to armed entry across a vast category of premises held open to the public, thereby burdening conduct the Second Amendment’s text plainly covers under Bruen. Under Bruen, the State must justify that sweeping, state-imposed consent-default with a well-established historical analogue; as Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, the proffered support is late and outlier-driven (including reliance on a Black Code), which cannot establish a mainstream founding-era tradition. Tyler, as multiple colleagues note, reinforces the anti-evasion principle: the State cannot manipulate background property/trespass baselines to accomplish indirectly what it lacks historical authority to do directly—effectively negating ordinary public carry. The practical consequences also cut against Hawaii: conditioning lawful carry on ad hoc permissions at routine commercial destinations functionally converts a right into a permission-slip regime without the historical pedigree Bruen requires.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s central claim is that Hawaii has "flipped the baseline" and must therefore produce a founding-era historical analogue under Bruen, and they invoke Tyler as an anti-evasion principle. I remain unpersuaded that Tyler supplies a general constitutional rule against a State’s setting default trespass terms for entry onto private property; Tyler concerned government appropriating value by redefining property rights, whereas here the State is mediating the owner’s right to exclude in a way that still permits carry where consent is given (including through posted policies) and does not resemble the discretionary licensing schemes Bruen condemned. Even accepting Bruen’s framework, the better characterization is not a sweeping "sensitive places" ban but a property-based default about the conditions of invitation onto another’s premises—an area where States have long set background rules—and the historical inquiry should be calibrated to that tradition rather than to categorical public-place disarmament. I also do not think the practical-burden arguments from Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Kagan are one-way: requiring affirmative consent in high-traffic commercial settings can modestly reduce foreseeable harms to vulnerable populations while preserving owner autonomy and leaving ample alternatives for lawful carry.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Hawaii is simply choosing a trespass-style default that respects owners’ right to exclude, and that Tyler should not be turned into a freestanding anti-baseline-shift principle. But as Chief Justice Roberts frames it, this is not ordinary trespass enforcement triggered by an owner’s objection; it is a State-imposed, across-the-board presumption of criminality for armed entry into the everyday places people are otherwise invited to enter, which under Bruen requires a well-established, representative historical analogue that Hawaii has not supplied. Tyler is not dispositive, but it supports the narrower proposition Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize: courts should be skeptical of statutory relabeling that functionally converts a constitutional baseline into a permission requirement without historical grounding. I therefore remain for the petitioner on a narrow holding limited to private property held open to the public, preserving owners’ ability to exclude through notice and ordinary trespass law.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument is that Hawaii is simply setting a trespass-style default to vindicate owners’ autonomy, not declaring a “sensitive place” or licensing regime, and she is right that Tyler is not a Second Amendment case and does not create a free-floating ban on all baseline shifts. But under Bruen the dispositive point remains that the State has attached criminal liability to the ordinary act of carrying on broad categories of property held open to the public—flipping the baseline from “lawful entry unless excluded” to “presumptively criminal absent affirmative consent”—and the State must justify that government-imposed burden with a well-established historical analogue, not a relabeling as property law. As Chief Justice Roberts persuasively suggests, we can resolve this narrowly: invalidate the affirmative-consent default as applied to ordinary public-facing commercial premises while preserving owners’ ability to exclude by notice and leaving genuinely sensitive places for another day. Sotomayor’s emphasis on real-time consent does not cure the constitutional defect because a permission-on-demand regime is itself the burden, and Hawaii’s late, outlier, and discriminatory historical sources cannot satisfy Bruen’s demand for a representative tradition.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Hawaii is just choosing a trespass-style default to respect owners’ traditional right to exclude, and she is right that Tyler is not itself a Second Amendment case. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, this statute is not ordinary trespass enforcement after notice; it is a statewide presumption of criminality for carrying on the vast run of premises held open to the public, which under Bruen requires a well-established, representative historical analogue—something the State has not supplied beyond late and outlier sources. Even accepting Sotomayor’s framing, the practical effect is to convert public carry into a permission-slip regime in the everyday places people “lawfully go,” which is exactly the kind of place-based burden Bruen treats as constitutionally significant. Tyler matters here only in the limited, anti-evasion sense Roberts and Justice Thomas identify: the State cannot evade constitutional scrutiny by redefining background rules in a targeted way that uniquely burdens the exercise of a constitutional right.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize that owners have a common-law right to exclude, and States may structure trespass defaults in many contexts; but Bruen requires Hawaii to justify a State-imposed presumption of criminality for bearing arms on property open to the public with a well-established historical analogue, not merely by labeling the restriction a property rule. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, flipping the baseline for ordinary commercial premises where the public is invited functions as a broad location-based prohibition on covered conduct and cannot be sustained on late, outlier evidence. Sotomayor’s attempt to distinguish Tyler as limited to takings does not persuade me, because Tyler supports the more modest anti-evasion proposition that government cannot redefine background legal baselines in a targeted way that uniquely burdens a constitutional right and thereby sidesteps the required constitutional showing. A narrow disposition—invalidating the affirmative-consent default as applied to private property held open to the public while preserving owners’ ability to exclude by notice—best fits the text, history, and precedent without opining on genuine sensitive-place regulations.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Hawaii is simply setting a trespass-style default to vindicate owners’ right to exclude, but that framing still leaves the State with Bruen’s threshold problem: it has imposed a statewide presumption of criminality on carrying in ordinary places open to the public, and it must justify that location-based burden with a well-established historical analogue, not with a relabeling as “property law.” Chief Justice Roberts persuasively explains why “on-the-spot consent” is not a constitutional baseline: it predictably converts a right into a permission regime at routine destinations and creates serious workability and fairness concerns for ordinary people trying to comply. Justice Kagan’s point about the State’s thin and late historical evidence (including outlier and discriminatory sources) reinforces that Hawaii has not carried its burden under Bruen’s representative-tradition demand. Tyler is not directly controlling, but it usefully underscores an anti-evasion principle relevant here: the State cannot redefine default rules in a way that uniquely burdens the exercise of a constitutional right while avoiding the historically grounded justification Bruen requires.

John Roberts.reasoning: Bruen holds that once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers carrying a handgun for self-defense in public, the State must justify a location-based restriction by pointing to a well-established, “relevantly similar” historical analogue—not a few outlier or discriminatory enactments—and Hawaii’s default presumption criminalizing carry on most private property open to the public unless the owner affirmatively consents functions as a broad place-based ban without the requisite historical pedigree. Treating ordinary businesses open to the public as presumptively off-limits effectively shrinks the practical right to “bear” arms recognized in Heller and applied to the States in McDonald, and Hawaii cannot evade that scrutiny by relabeling the regime as merely a trespass baseline when the State itself has altered the default rule in a way that burdens a constitutional right (cf. Tyler’s insistence that government cannot redefine background property rules to avoid constitutional limits). For institutional reasons, I would decide narrowly: invalidate the statute as applied to private property “open to the public” to the extent it imposes a statewide default no-carry rule absent affirmative consent, while leaving intact the ability of owners to exclude by posting or direct notice and leaving sensitive-place questions for another day under Bruen.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text protects the right to “bear” arms in public for self-defense, and Hawaii’s default rule—criminalizing carry on vast swaths of private property held open to the public unless the owner gives affirmative consent—directly burdens that covered conduct. Under Bruen’s text-and-history test, Hawaii must identify a well-established founding-era tradition of a government-imposed consent-default for such premises, and reliance on postbellum outliers (including discriminatory Black Codes) cannot supply the requisite “mainstream” tradition. Nor may the State evade Second Amendment scrutiny by redefining baseline trespass/property rules to shift the default in a way that effectively nullifies ordinary public carry, a maneuver inconsistent with the principle that government cannot manipulate background property rules to burden a constitutional right (see Tyler v. Hennepin County). Because Hawaii has not carried its historical burden, Haw. Rev. Stat. § 134-9.5 violates the Second Amendment as incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Hawaii’s default rule makes it presumptively criminal to “bear Arms” on vast amounts of private property that is open to the public, so the Second Amendment’s plain text covers the regulated conduct and the State bears the burden under Bruen to justify the restriction by a well-established historical analogue. Under N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022), the State cannot defend what functionally negates ordinary public carry by pointing to scattered, late, or discriminatory outliers—particularly reliance on an 1865 Black Code—rather than a mainstream founding-era tradition. Nor may the State evade Second Amendment scrutiny by redefining baseline trespass/property rules to impose a broad, location-based carry ban on the public; as Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023), illustrates in the property context, government cannot manipulate background property rules to sidestep constitutional constraints. Practical consequences reinforce that this regime will chill lawful carry by making routine stops at stores, gas stations, and inns presumptively criminal unless individualized consent is obtained.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Hawaii’s statute is best understood as a regulation that mediates between the Second Amendment and the long-settled common-law power of private owners to exclude others from their premises, including premises held open to the public, and it does so by setting a default that preserves owner choice rather than creating a blanket “sensitive place” prohibition. Even accepting Bruen’s text-and-history framework, 597 U.S. 1 (2022), the State’s approach is materially narrower than the kind of near-total public-carry nullification Bruen condemned, because it permits carry where owners consent (including on-the-spot oral consent) and does not impose discretionary licensing criteria. Petitioners’ Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023), “anti-evasion” analogy is inapt: Hawaii is not confiscating a constitutional entitlement by redefining property to seize value; it is using trespass-style defaults to respect property owners’ autonomy while leaving the right to bear arms intact in public spaces not owned by unwilling private parties. Given the real-world risks of firearms in densely used commercial settings and the State’s broad remedial authority to protect public safety without foreclosing self-defense categorically, I would uphold the regime as a permissible accommodation rather than a Second Amendment violation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers carrying firearms in public for self-defense, Hawaii must justify its presumptive ban on carrying on private property held open to the public by pointing to a well-established, mainstream historical analogue, not by invoking modern policy judgments or outlier postbellum enactments like an 1865 Black Code. Hawaii’s regime flips the common-law baseline for places of public accommodation—treating ordinary entry as lawful but armed entry as presumptively criminal unless the owner affirmatively speaks—thereby functionally burdening ordinary public carry across large swaths of daily life in a way the State has not shown to be consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition. Nor can the State evade Second Amendment scrutiny by recasting this as mere enforcement of owners’ exclusion rights; as Tyler v. Hennepin County illustrates, government may not manipulate baseline property rules to sidestep constitutional constraints, and here the State’s default rule operates as a state-imposed disarmament presumption. Because the asserted historical support is thin, late, and contested, and the rule’s workability problems are substantial in practice, I would hold the law unconstitutional as applied to private property open to the public.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text protects the right to “bear Arms,” and under Bruen that presumptively covers carrying firearms for self-defense in ordinary places one may lawfully go, including commercial premises open to the public. Hawaii’s default rule flips the traditional baseline by making carry on vast swaths of publicly accessible private property presumptively criminal absent affirmative consent, effectively converting the right to bear arms into a permission slip regime—something the State must justify with a well-established, mainstream historical analogue, not policy balancing. Bruen rejects reliance on outlier or discriminatory postbellum enactments as proof of the Nation’s tradition, and an 1865 Louisiana Black Code cannot supply the needed pedigree; nor may the State evade Second Amendment scrutiny by “redefining” property/trespass defaults to burden a constitutional right, a principle consistent with Tyler v. Hennepin County’s insistence that government cannot manipulate background property rules to defeat constitutional protections. On this record, Hawaii has not carried its historical burden, so the regime violates the Second Amendment as incorporated by the Fourteenth Amendment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text covers carrying handguns in public for self-defense, and Hawaii’s default rule—making it presumptively criminal to carry on vast categories of private property open to the public absent affirmative consent—functions as a broad location-based restriction on bearing arms. Under Bruen, the State must justify such a restriction by pointing to a well-established, representative historical tradition of comparable regulation, and reliance on outlier postbellum sources such as discriminatory Black Codes cannot supply the “mainstream” analogue Bruen requires. Nor may the State evade Second Amendment scrutiny by redefining baseline property/trespass rules in a way that uniquely burdens a constitutional right, a principle consistent with this Court’s refusal to allow government manipulation of property baselines to avoid constitutional constraints (see Tyler v. Hennepin County). The regime’s practical workability concerns—requiring individualized permission at ordinary commercial premises—underscore that it is not a narrow “sensitive places” regulation recognized in Heller and Bruen but instead a near-default disarmament rule in public life.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text protects an individual’s right to “bear Arms” in public for self-defense, and Hawaii’s default rule makes that covered conduct presumptively criminal across the vast universe of privately owned places open to the public. Under Bruen’s text-and-history test, the State must identify a well-established historical analogue from the relevant tradition; the cited anti-poaching/trespass measures limited to private lands not held open to the public and Reconstruction-era outliers like the 1865 Louisiana Black Code do not supply the required mainstream tradition, and Bruen instructs courts to discount such outliers. Nor may the State evade Second Amendment scrutiny by redefining background property/trespass rules to burden a constitutional right, a principle consistent with Tyler v. Hennepin County’s refusal to let government manipulate property baselines to avoid constitutional constraints. Because Hawaii’s presumption functionally forecloses ordinary public carry in common destinations without a historically grounded analogue, it violates the Second Amendment as incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers carrying arms for self-defense in public, Hawaii must justify its default criminalization of carry on private property open to the public by demonstrating a well-established historical analogue; the record described in argument points instead to sparse, postbellum, and even discriminatory sources (e.g., an 1865 Black Code), which cannot supply the “mainstream” tradition Bruen demands. The State’s reframing of the law as mere vindication of owners’ right to exclude does not avoid constitutional scrutiny where the government itself creates a presumption of illegality that predictably burdens ordinary carry across vast swaths of daily life—an anti-manipulation concern akin to Tyler v. Hennepin County’s insistence that States cannot redefine baseline property rules to evade constitutional limits. As a matter of practical consequences and procedural fairness, conditioning lawful carry on ad hoc, on-the-spot permissions at every store or gas station functionally transforms a constitutional right into a permission regime, which Bruen and McDonald reject as interest-balancing by another name. Hawaii remains free to enforce traditional trespass law where an owner actually forbids firearms and to regulate genuinely “sensitive places,” but this blanket default presumption fails the Second Amendment test as incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment.
